item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It was me, actually. I was active on the old website and wrote several, including Infinite Speed Computer, Ash Bacteria, and SCP-974 (Deadly Image) . This is the only one to live, so thanks for the rewrite.

The latter was a very rudimentary cognitohazard - cognitohazards weren't as cliche back then, but still I'm not surprised it was deleted. To my excuse, I was 14 at the time. There's a twist to the story though. When I was thinking of countermeasures against cognitohazards, I invented the idea of Class A and Class C amnesiacs, which has since become a key part of the canon, though now they're more usually called 'amnestics'. It's very curious how some crappy article I wrote when I was 14 contributed a term which is now famous, and it makes me quite proud.

Now, after nearly a decade, I'm back to the wiki to write some more things.

item.content:encoded:
True. My initial thoughts were that timing might not be possible depending on the hardware it was running on, but then I realised it lists it in the description as a real-life model of supercomputer, meaning it is trivial to get a full operating system working on it. Although, if I understand the way the warp works, you'd need to code it to terminate after a certain amount of time in-bubble, not out-bubble (eg. a hundred years instead of 8m14s).

Also, as to your example, you could save the program's state after a certain time, then restart the computer and resume at that state, essentially giving you a controlled burst of radiation every so often, though it does increase (real-time) runtime.

As to why they don't just terminate after a time:
As a maths student turned software engineer, there's something you need to know about (most) mathematicians. If you give them a problem where something needs to not run infinitely, they will naturally set about formally proving that all programs are non-halting. It would never occur to them to simply force kill it after a certain time.
So consider it an in-universe oversight because the researchers are formalists, not engineers :P

(Pre-emptively: Not implying engineers are superior. Just noting that people like the mathematicians I know could feasibly make this mistake.)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I hated the old version of this — as someone who actually programs for a living, it rubbed me the wrong way. This new one deals with all of my major complaints about the old version in splendid fashion.

However, I feel it necessary to point out that a huge percentage of the programs researchers would like to run on this thing involve cases where we don't know if the program is an infinite loop or not. In other words, you're trying to determine whether (say) there exists a number which satisfies condition X. So, given that you have an infinite-speed computer, you write the equivalent of the following pseudocode:

x = 1
loop:
if x satisfies condition X then
print "The answer is: " + x
halt
else
x = x + 1
goto loop
end if

In other words, this program eventually halts if such a number exists, and doesn't halt if such a number doesn't exist. Since we have absolutely no idea whether this is the case or not and the slightest mistake in coding it can easily leave you with an infinite loop (which are one of the more common programming errors), the fact that there are absolutely no safeguards around this bothers me. Seems like you should have a hard stop after however many minutes so we don't blow up the building anytime somebody makes a typo or a mathematical conjecture doesn't pan out. I'm completely fine with the first explosion, as we presumably didn't know that that would happen, but we know now and should have safeguards against it.

item.content:encoded:
This is a minor thing, and it may just be me being too maths-nerd, but it completely threw me off when I first read it, so I thought I'd mention it:
You say that the effective processing power exponentially increases. However you also say "its effective processing power approaches infinity after approximately 8 minutes and 14 seconds of execution". If I understand you correctly, you're implying that there exists a vertical asymptote, and the processing power gets arbitrarily high as you get closer to t=8m14s, or:

$\displaystyle \lim_{t \rightarrow 8m14s} {\rm Power} = \infty$

This isn't possible with a strictly exponential pattern of increase, no matter what constants are involved.
I suggest a change from "resulting in an exponential increase" to "resulting in a hyperbolic increase", ie:
${\rm Power} = \frac{1}{8m14s - t}$
Graph here: http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=plot+1+%2F+%28494+-+x%29+from+0+to+494

(also: The wiki markup gives me $\LaTeX$ math rendering? That's $\mathbb{AWESOME}$.)

After some internal deliberation, I decided that I couldn't let the Infinite Speed Computer die without a fight. So, I have massively rewritten it from scratch, and attributed its creation to Prometheus Labs.

Long live the oldies!

Edit: I pulled up the archives in an attempt to give proper credit to the original author of SCP-155, only to find that it was posted on July 28, 2008 by Anonymous back when the wiki was an open wiki. The world may never know.
